hook_text: 50 millilitres of water plus 50 millilitres of alcohol makes 96 millilitres. Nothing spilled. Nothing evaporated. The missing four is proof that everything is full of holes.
clip_script: Measure 50 millilitres of water. Add 50 millilitres of alcohol. Mix. Read the cylinder: about 96. Where did four millilitres go? Nowhere. Everything is made of tiny particles with empty space between them, and when the two liquids mix, some particles slip into the gaps between others, like marbles poured into a bucket of tennis balls. That is the particle model. Particles, empty space, constant motion, and forces pulling them together. Now picture a school day. Assembly is a solid: everyone in fixed rows, close together, fidgeting on the spot. Break in a packed corridor is a liquid: still close, but sliding past each other, so it flows. Home time on the field is a gas: everyone sprinting in every direction, far apart, filling the whole space. Same learners all day. Only the spacing and the speed change. One millilitre of water boils into about seventeen hundred millilitres of steam: same particles, just far, far apart.
visual_style: A whiteboard measuring cylinder reading 96 with a question mark; then marbles settling into a bucket of tennis balls; then three boxes of same-sized circles for solid, liquid and gas.
pacing: A puzzling opening, a clean reveal, a lively school-day analogy and a big-number finish.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and draw all three states correctly.
